summary: For ages 5–7: whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish, because they breathe air at the surface, are warm-blooded, and feed their babies milk — even though they live in the ocean. The teaching target is classification BY FEATURE, deliberately confronting the 'lives in water = fish' misconception. The lead activity has the child run a mammal feature-checklist against several sea animals and sort them; supporting activities provide a side-by-side mammal/fish contrast, an assessment sort, and an optional in-role dialogue spark.
misconceptions: 'It lives in water and swims, so it's a fish' — the core habitat-equals-category error this topic exists to fix.
'It has fins, so it's a fish' — classifying by superficial body shape rather than defining features.
'Mammals can't live in water / can't hold their breath that long' — not knowing whales surface to breathe air.
'A shark is a mammal because it's big/smart' — over-applying the new category; sharks are fish (gills, no milk).
Thinking 'warm-blooded' means the animal feels warm to touch, rather than regulating its own body temperature.

activities.title: Sort the sea animals by feature, not by where they live
steps: Meet a line-up of sea animals — dolphin, whale, seal, shark, cod, clownfish — each shown with tappable feature clues (surfaces to breathe / has gills / calf nursing / lays eggs / keeps its body warm even in cold water).

For each animal, tick the features you find and use a simple checklist to decide: does it come up to breathe air? does it feed its baby milk? does its body stay warm even in cold water? does it have gills?
Drop each animal into the MAMMAL box or the FISH box based on the ticked features, not on the fact that it swims in the sea.

Try the dolphin: tap its blowhole to see it surface and breathe air, and tap the nursing calf — then deliberately leave the shark (it breathes with gills and does not feed its babies milk) in the FISH box to avoid over-generalising.
State out loud: 'A dolphin is a mammal, and two reasons are ___ and ___.'
activities.insight: The rule that decides mammal vs fish is the animal's defining FEATURES (breathes air, feeds milk, warm-blooded) — not its habitat or body shape. The same test applies to a brand-new animal.

activities.title: Side-by-side: dolphin vs fish, reveal the matching features
steps: Look at a split scene: a dolphin (with blowhole and nursing calf, and that stays warm in cold water) beside a real fish (with gills, eggs, scales).
Tap each hotspot to lift a flap — tap the blowhole → 'breathes air'; tap the calf → 'drinks milk'; tap the gills → 'breathes using water through gills'; tap the eggs → 'lays eggs'.
Say which trait on the dolphin matches which trait on the fish, pairing each mammal feature with its fish counterpart.
activities.insight: Mammals and fish differ by traits that can be compared one-to-one (blowhole vs gills, milk vs eggs for most fish, keeps-warm vs cold-blooded for most fish), so the categories are set by features, not by where the animal lives.

activities.title: Check and extend: sort, say why, and test a new animal
steps: Sort a fresh set of animals into mammal vs fish.
Answer 'Why is a dolphin a mammal?' choosing the feature-based reason (breathes air / feeds milk) over a habitat reason.
Tackle a transfer question: 'Is a shark a mammal?' and give the reason from its features (breathes with gills, does not feed its babies milk → fish).
activities.insight: The learner can independently justify the category with defining features and apply the test to an animal they were not taught directly.

activities.title: Optional spark: ask the dolphin why it keeps surfacing
steps: Talk in role to a friendly dolphin (or a marine biologist) and ask 'Why do you keep coming up to the top of the water?'
Hear the dolphin explain: 'I have to breathe air like you — that's why I'm not a fish,' and ask a follow-up about how its baby feeds.
activities.insight: The air-breathing proof becomes memorable and personal — the dolphin is 'like us', not like a fish.

checkQuestion: A dolphin lives in the sea, swims fast, and has fins and a smooth tail. A child says: 'So a dolphin must be a fish.' Is that right? Tell me what a dolphin really is, and how you can tell.
checkAnswer: It's not right — a dolphin (and a whale) is a MAMMAL, not a fish, even though it lives in the sea. You can tell because it breathes AIR: it has to come up to the surface to breathe and cannot breathe underwater. It is also warm-blooded, and it feeds its babies milk. Living in water and having fins does not make an animal a fish.
